places.summary: A rough plank saloon by the rail yard: whiskey from a barrel, a mirror with a bullet hole and a sign saying don't shoot the piano player.
The fanciest saloon in the territory, with chandeliers, an orchestra in the gallery and roulette until dawn.
A cool adobe cantina with mescal, guitars on Saturday night and a courtyard under a grape arbour.
The German brewer's beer garden with lager, pretzels, a brass band on Sundays and long tables under the trees.
A stone stage station where the coach changes horses, with a hot meal for the passengers and bunks for the drivers.
Bunks by the shift: the day man sleeps while the night man works, and the landlady keeps the sheets turning.
Steak, beans, biscuits and coffee strong enough to float a horseshoe, served at a counter to anybody with two bits.
A restaurant with white tablecloths and oysters packed in ice on the train, so the mine owners can pretend they are in San Francisco.
Ice cream, lemonade and sarsaparilla at a marble counter, the one place in town a lady can sit without a fuss.
Sacks of oats and barley, seed corn, harness and the latest prices chalked on a board by the door.
Farmers' wagons round the plaza with melons, chiles, eggs and goat cheese, and a man selling patent medicine off a tailboard.
Barbed wire, stoves, rifles, windmill parts and a catalogue you can order anything else from.
Hats with feathers from back East, patterns from Godey's and a dressmaker who can copy anything from a picture.
Blankets, silver, baskets and pottery traded by Navajo, Apache and Pueblo families, alongside coffee and flour.
Patent medicines, cigars, stationery, toilet water and the only telephone in town, in a store that smells of camphor.
A small temple kept by the Chinese community, red and gold inside, with incense burning before the altar.
A variety theatre with boxes round the walls, dancers, comics and a poker game that has been going for weeks.
Where the travelling Wild West show sets up: trick riders, sharpshooters and a stagecoach chase twice a day.
The brick courthouse with a clock tower and a jail behind, where trials draw bigger crowds than the opera house.
The railroad depot and water tower, where the whole town meets the daily train for mail, news and strangers.
The hillside graveyard of wooden markers, some with jokes on them, where the town's early arguments were settled for good.
A tall steel windmill pumping water to the town trough, creaking all night when the wind is up.
A grove of cottonwoods along the creek where the Fourth of July picnic, baseball and church socials happen.
A switchback trail up onto the mesa for the sunset, the view of the whole valley and the old cliff dwellings.
The old wagon road along the river, rutted by the first emigrant trains, now for buggy rides and courting.
Bath houses over natural hot springs, said to cure rheumatism, gout and most of what ails a miner.
A dirt diamond where the town nine plays the next town's nine on Sundays, with a lot of money changing hands.
The livery stable's horse doctor, who will see to a lame horse, a cow with colic or a dog with porcupine quills.
A Yorkshire-style beerhouse where the brass band practises upstairs on Tuesdays and the whippet club meets on Fridays.
An old timbered pub that Dickens is supposed to have stayed in, and the landlord will tell you about it.
Pie, mash and liquor, jellied eels and tiled walls, with the queue out the door at dinnertime.
A Soho-style Italian place with macaroni, chianti in straw bottles and artists who pay in sketches.
Hot cocoa, bread and dripping and a fire to sit by, set up by the vicar's wife to keep working men out of the pub.
Tea from an urn, stale buns, a fire in the grate and a waiting room full of people who have missed their train.
Second-hand clothes, boots, buttons and old iron, sold off barrows and blankets on Sunday morning.
The workers' co-operative store, groceries to coal, paying a dividend each quarter that everybody counts on.
New novels in three volumes, penny dreadfuls under the counter and a subscription library at the back.
A wooden Highlander at the door, jars of shag and cavendish, and gentlemen arguing politics by the counter.
A Gothic hall of dinosaur skeletons, beetles pinned in drawers and a whale's jaw over the door.
A great hall with an organ, oratorios at Christmas and a choral society that sings the Messiah every year.
Seances, table-rapping and lectures on ectoplasm, with a medium who is never wrong about anything that can't be checked.
A cast-iron clock tower put up for the Jubilee, where everybody arranges to meet and everybody is late.
A temple of brass columns turning day and night, working out tide tables, gunnery and the census.
A gift to the town of trees from every corner of the Empire, with a pagoda, a lake and keepers in bowler hats.
A darkened room on the hilltop where a lens throws the whole town, moving, onto a white table.
A novelty railway that whooshes carriages along a tube by air pressure, a penny a go and never quite on time.
A brewery that fills the street with the smell of malt, its dray horses the best fed in town.
Hot rooms, a plunge pool and a cooling room of cane chairs, ladies' days on Tuesday and Friday.
A cinder cycle track and club house, where the new safety bicycles race and ladies in bloomers scandalise the vicar.
